notes.short: Like Nicodemus, she may take His picture literally
notes.about: Jesus offers living water, and the woman answers, “You have nothing to draw with and the well is deep.” Told he must be born again, Nicodemus asked, “How can a man be born when he is old?” Each answer can be read as taking His picture of spiritual life as an earthly thing.

sides.label: Answers with the well and its depth
sides.words: You have nothing to draw with and the well is deep.

sides.label: Thinks of a second natural birth
sides.words: How can a man be born when he is old?

notes.evidence: Matthew Henry, on 4:11: what Jesus spoke figuratively she took literally, and Nicodemus did the same; both show how confused the notions of spiritual things are in people taken up with what the senses know.
notes.limit: Not all agree she missed His meaning: she may have seen the picture and mocked it. The likeness is only in how each first answered: she went on to tell her town about Jesus, and Nicodemus later spoke up for Him and helped bury Him.

cites.quote: What he spoke figuratively, she took literally; Nicodemus did so too. See what confused notions they have of spiritual things who are wholly taken up with the things that are sensible.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: Christ the vine, His disciples the branches
notes.about: Jesus pictures Himself as the vine and His disciples as its branches. A branch lives and bears fruit only while it is joined to the vine; so they bear fruit only by remaining in Him, and apart from Him they can do nothing.

figure.name: Metaphor
figure.words: I am the vine and you are the branches
figure.means: Christ, from whom His disciples draw all their life and fruit, as branches do from the vine

notes.evidence: Clarke speaks of following our Lord’s metaphor: no good can be done without Him, any more than a branch cut off from the tree can bear fruit. Barnes: as branches separated from the parent stock bear no fruit, so Christians separate from Christ can do nothing. Henry reads verses 1 to 8 as a similitude in which believers are the branches; Calvin calls the verse the application of the whole parable.

cites.quote: Following the metaphor of our Lord, it would be just as possible to do any good without him, as for a branch to live, thrive, and bring forth fruit, while cut off from that tree from which it not only derives its juices, but its very existence also.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: As the branches, if separated from the parent stock, could produce no fruit, but would immediately wither and die, so Christians, if separate from Christ, could do nothing.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Here Christ discourses concerning the fruit, the fruits of the Spirit, which his disciples were to bring forth, under the similitude of a vine. ... That believers are branches of this vine, which supposes that Christ is the root of the vine.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: This is the conclusion and application of the whole parable. So long as we are separate from him, we bear no fruit that is good and acceptable to God, for we are unable to do anything good.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.about: The word “nothing” is wide, but here it is narrowed to what the vine picture is about: apart from Christ His disciples can bear no fruit, and do nothing good or pleasing to God.

figure.name: Synecdoche
figure.means: nothing good or pleasing to God; the wide word is narrowed to the good fruit the verse speaks of

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Synecdoche of the Genus, where a universal negative does not deny every particular: nothing good, true and right. Brown (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) explains it as nothing done spiritually or acceptably; Calvin says that apart from Christ we bear no fruit good and acceptable to God.

cites.at: Synecdoche of the Genus: a universal negative, p. 619
cites.quote: “Without me ye can do nothing”: i.e., nothing that is good and true and right, or according to God; but a great deal that is contrary to Him.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: without me--apart, or vitally disconnected from Me. ye can do nothing--spiritually, acceptably.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: So long as we are separate from him, we bear no fruit that is good and acceptable to God, for we are unable to do anything good.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: “I will never drive away” means a sure welcome
notes.about: Jesus says He will never drive away the one who comes to Him. The words say less than they mean: He will not only refuse to turn such a one away but will receive him and keep him. John 10:28 makes the same promise: no one can snatch His sheep out of His hand.

figure.name: Tapeinosis
figure.means: He will surely receive the one who comes to Him and keep him

original.note: In John's Greek the negative is doubled (ou mē), so the promise is said with double force.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Tapeinosis: much more is meant than the words say, for Christ will receive, preserve and defend the one who comes. Bengel calls it a litotes whose meaning is stronger than its words: not only first welcome but lasting keeping. Henry notes the two negatives and says more favour is implied than expressed: Christ will receive those who come and not cast them out later.
notes.limit: Some writers take the words only as Christ's welcome to every sinner who comes, not also as a promise to keep him afterwards.

cites.quote: Here, there is very much more implied than is expressed in the literal words. Not only will I not cast him out, but I will by all means receive him and preserve him, and defend him: he shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck him out of My hand.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: This signifies not merely the first reception, but the lasting preservation ... There is a Litotes [the meaning is stronger than the literal words]: I will not cast him out, but by all means will preserve him;
cites.read: Bible Hub's transcription, at https://biblehub.com/commentaries/bengel/john/6.htm

cites.quote: There are two negatives: I will not, no, I will not. ... More favour is implied than is expressed; when it is said that he will no cast them out the meaning is, He will receive them, and entertain them, and give them all that which they come to him for. As he will not refuse them at their first coming, so he will not afterwards, upon every displeasure, cast them out.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: A challenge none of His accusers could answer
notes.about: Jesus asks which of His hearers can prove Him guilty of sin. He does not ask to learn but to challenge them, knowing that none of them could. Then He presses the point: if He speaks the truth, why do they not believe Him?

figure.name: Erotesis
figure.words: Which of you can prove Me guilty of sin?
figure.means: none of you can convict Me of any sin

original.note: In John's Greek the verb is elencho: not to persuade but to convict, to prove guilty and lay bare.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists it under Erotesis, in Affirmative Negation: no one could ever convict Christ of sin. Calvin says it comes from full confidence that they could bring no just charge. Henry calls it a challenge and their charges groundless. Brown (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls it a challenge claiming absolute sinlessness; Watkins (Ellicott) says no one dared answer.
notes.limit: The writers differ on how far the challenge reaches: some take it as a claim to be wholly without sin, while others read it more narrowly, as a challenge to fault His teaching or His life as God's servant.

cites.quote: “Which of you convicteth me of sin?” (Joh 8:46 ). ἐλέγχω ( elengcho ) does not mean to convince , but to convict by bringing in guilty, lay bare, expose . No one could ever bring Christ in guilty of sin.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: This question proceeds from perfect confidence; for, knowing that they could not justly bring any reproach against him, he glories over his enemies, as having obtained a victory.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: But their accusations were malicious groundless calumnies, and such as every one that knew him knew to be utterly false. ... The sin he here challenges them to convict him of is, First, An inconsistent doctrine. ... Or, Secondly, An incongruous conversation: "Which of you can justly charge me with any thing, in word or deed, unbecoming a prophet?"
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: such a challenge thrown wide among His bitterest enemies, can amount to nothing short of a claim to absolute sinlessness.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: It is an appeal that spotless purity alone could make ... We may suppose that the last question was probably followed by a pause, during which any one might have answered the challenge. No one of all who had watched Him in Galilee and Judæa dared utter a syllable.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: A world too small for the books: more than literal
notes.about: John closes by saying the world itself would not have space for the books if all that Jesus did were written down. The words say more than is meant literally: far more was done than could ever be recorded, and what is written was chosen so that we may believe (John 20:31).

figure.name: Hyperbole
figure.words: not even the world itself would have space for the books that would be written
figure.means: that Jesus did far more than could ever be written down: a vast number of books would be needed

original.note: In John's Greek the verb for “have space” is chōreō, to make room for or take in, the verb Matthew 19:11 uses for accepting a word.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Hyperbole and takes the verb as in Matthew 19:11. Barnes calls it a hyperbole meaning only that a great many books would be needed, John giving just what proves Jesus the Messiah. Henry calls it a justifiable hyperbole for a vast number of volumes, and Calvin defends it as an ordinary figure commending the greatness of Christ's works.
notes.limit: Some read the words more literally, as John's plain word that his material was far from exhausted. Some take “have space” as to receive, as in Matthew 19:11, so that mankind could not take in so many books.

cites.quote: Joh 21:25 is also Hyperbole. The verb χωρῆσαι (chōreesai) is to be taken in the same sense, as it is in Mat 19:11, where the Lord says, “All men cannot receive this saying;”
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: This is evidently the figure of speech called a hyperbole. It is a mode of speech where the words express more or less than is literally true. ... he clearly intends nothing more than that a great many books would be required ... that he had not pretended to give them all, but only such as would go to establish the main point for which he wrote that he was the Messiah
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The world could not contain the books. It is a hyperbole common enough and justifiable, when no more is intended than this, that it would fill a vast and incredible number of volumes.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: nor ought we to think that the hyperbole is absurd ... If the Evangelist, casting his eyes on that brightness, exclaims in astonishment, that even the whole world could not contain a full narrative, ought we to wonder at it? Nor is he at all to be blamed, if he employ a frequent and ordinary figure of speech for commending the excellence of the works of Christ.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: A common saying that scorned Nazareth
notes.about: Nathanael answers with what seems to have been a common saying of the day, scorning the town of Nazareth: could the Messiah come from such a place? Philip does not argue but says, “Come and see.” Nathanael comes, and Jesus calls him a true Israelite.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.part: Quoted as being already in use as such
figure.words: Can anything good come from Nazareth?
figure.means: a common, scornful saying that nothing good comes from Nazareth, here turned against Jesus, who grew up there

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the question under Parœmia among proverbs quoted as already in use, which he says John 7:41-42 and 7:52 show. Benson calls it a proverb by which other Israelites ridiculed the Nazarenes, and says Nathanael applied it because Micah had named Bethlehem as the Messiah's birthplace.
notes.limit: The verse does not itself call the question a saying. Nathanael may also have had in mind that Scripture named Bethlehem, not Nazareth, as the Messiah's birthplace.

cites.at: Parœmiœ which are quoted as being already in use as such, p. 757
cites.quote: This appears from 7:41, 42, 52, to have been a proverb already in use.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: A proverb, by which the rest of the Israelites ridiculed the Nazarenes. Nathanael, on this occasion, applied it the rather, because the Messiah's nativity had been determined by the Prophet Micah to Bethlehem. ... it appears from hence that the Galileans themselves had but an ill opinion of Nazareth, as worse than the rest of that country
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: “This temple” stands for His body, left unsaid
notes.about: Jesus says, “Destroy this temple,” without saying that He means His body, and His hearers think of the building. John explains that He was speaking about the temple of His body (verse 21). The saying foretold His death at their hands and His rising in three days.

figure.name: Hypocatastasis
figure.means: His own body, which they would put to death and He would raise up in three days

original.note: In John's Greek the word is naos, the sanctuary itself rather than the whole temple area.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Hypocatastasis: Jesus did not say His body was like the temple or was the temple, but only implied the word body. Calvin calls the saying allegorical; Henry says Jesus foretold His death and rising in figurative words; Barnes and H. W. Watkins (Ellicott's Commentary) explain why His body is called a temple.

cites.quote: The Lord Jesus did not say that His body was like the temple (that would have been Simile), or that it was His body (that would have been Metaphor). He merely implied the word body, as ver. 21 plainly declares
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: This is an allegorical mode of expression; and Christ intentionally spoke with that degree of obscurity, because he reckoned them unworthy of a direct reply … Though he uses the word temple in accommodation to the present occurrence, yet the body of Christ is justly and appropriately called a temple.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: He foretels his death and resurrection, not in plain terms, as he often did to his disciples, but in figurative expressions … Note, The body of Christ is the true temple, of which that at Jerusalem was a type.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Our Saviour called his body a temple in accordance with the common use of language … As the Lord Jesus was divine - as the fulness of the Godhead dwelt in him so his body might be called a "temple."
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The enigma turns in the present case upon the double sense of the word “temple.” It meant the sacred shrine of the Deity, the Holy and Most Holy place, as distinct from the wider Temple area. But the true shrine of the Deity was the body of the Incarnate Word.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: Moses' raised snake pictures the Son lifted up
notes.about: Jesus sets the bronze snake Moses raised on a pole beside His own lifting up. Many read the snake as a type: as each bitten Israelite who looked at it lived, so “everyone who believes in Him may have eternal life” (3:15).

figure.name: Type
figure.words: Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness
figure.means: the bronze snake on its pole, pointing ahead to the Son of Man lifted up, so that whoever looks to Him in faith lives

notes.evidence: Henry calls the bronze snake a type of Christ: shaped like the serpents yet without poison, as Christ was made sin yet knew no sin. Calvin says Jesus refers to it as a type of His own lifting up. The Catena Aurea of Thomas Aquinas gives Bede, who says the story was meant as a figure of His Passion and of man's salvation.
notes.limit: John 12:32-33 ties the lifting up to His death; one writer reads it here as Christ set forth before all in the preaching of the gospel.

cites.quote: Now in this type of Christ we may observe, First, The deadly and destructive nature of sin ... It was made in the shape of a fiery serpent, and yet had no poison, no sting, fitly representing Christ, who was made sin for us and yet knew no sin
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The simple meaning of the words therefore is, that, by the preaching of the Gospel, Christ was to be raised on high, like a standard to which the eyes of all would be directed ... As a type of this lifting up, he refers to the brazen serpent, which was erected by Moses, the sight of which was a salutary remedy to those who had been wounded by the deadly bite of serpents.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: He introduces the teacher of the Mosaic law, to the spiritual sense of that law; by a passage from the Old Testament history, which was intended to be a figure of His Passion, and of man’s salvation.
cites.read: Newman's Oxford translation, in the copy at github.com/AlvaroBalbin/catena (commit efe1bd0)

notes.short: “One sows and another reaps”: an old saying
notes.about: Jesus quotes a common saying and says it is true here: others did the hard work, and the disciples reap the harvest (verse 38). The saying often spoke of loss, but here the sower and the reaper rejoice together (verse 36).

figure.name: Proverb
figure.part: Quoted as being already in use as such
figure.means: one labors and another gathers the fruit; the sowers are read as the prophets before Christ, and the reapers as His disciples

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Parœmia among proverbs quoted as already in use. Calvin and Benson both call it a common proverb, and both say that, unlike its common use, here the sower does not grudge the reaper but shares his joy. Clarke says the proverb is taken from what often happens, one taking pains for what another reaps, and reads the sowers as the patriarchs and prophets.
notes.limit: The verses do not name the sowers.

cites.at: Parœmiœ which are quoted as being already in use as such, p. 757
cites.quote: Parœmiœ which are quoted as being already in use as such ... “And herein is that saying true; ‘One soweth, and another reapeth.’ ”
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: This was a common proverb, by which he showed that many men frequently receive the fruit of the labor of others, though there was this difference, that he who has labored is displeased at seeing the fruit carried away by another, whereas the Apostles have the Prophets for the companions of their joy.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: That common proverb; One soweth and another reapeth He alludes to what often happens ... But the application which our Lord makes of this proverb here, does not imply any discontent in the persons who sow without reaping, as it seems to do in common uses; for the sower and the reaper are represented as rejoicing together
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: this proverb is true ... Others have labored - the patriarchs and prophets, and ye are entered into the fruits of their labors. ... The proverb which our Lord mentions above was taken from what ordinarily happens in the course of the Divine providence, where one takes a great deal of pains to procure that of which another reaps the benefit.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Jesus' words frame it; the Sabbath is at the centre
notes.about: The account goes out and comes back: the words of Jesus, the man made well, the mat carried, the Sabbath; then the Sabbath, the mat carried, the man made well, and the words of Jesus again, as the man repeats them.

lines.words: Get up, pick up your mat, and walk.
Immediately the man was made well,
and he picked up his mat and began to walk.
Now this happened on the Sabbath day,
It is unlawful for you to carry your mat.
The man who made me well
told me, ‘Pick up your mat and walk.’

notes.evidence: Boys and Bullinger both set out these verses in eight parts: the words of the Lord at the ends, then the man made whole, then the bed carried, and the Sabbath at the centre.

cites.quote: In d. and d., the sabbath; in c. and c., the bed carried; in b. and b., the man made whole; in a. and a., the words of our Lord.
cites.read: the 1824 printing, in the scan at archive.org/details/tactica-sacra

cites.quote: Here in A and A we have the words of Christ; in B and B the man made whole; in C and C the bed he carried; and in D and D the Sabbath.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

notes.short: Outer verses answer, and so do the inner two
notes.about: Verses 20 and 23 answer each other on the outside, and verses 21 and 22 answer each other in the middle: the Son gives life, and all judgment is given to the Son.

lines.words: The Father loves the Son and shows Him all He does.
so also the Son gives life to whom He wishes.
but has assigned all judgment to the Son,
so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father.

notes.evidence: Forbes, on verses 20 to 23: the two distichs of verse 20 correspond to the two of verse 23, while the two central verses, 21 and 22, correspond to each other.

cites.quote: The two distichs of v. 20 correspond to the two distichs of v. 23 respectively ... while the two central verses, 21 and 22, mutually correspond.
cites.read: the 1854 printing, in the scan at archive.org/details/symmetricalstruc00forbiala

notes.short: The manna pointed ahead to the true bread
notes.about: The crowd holds up the manna as bread from heaven. Jesus answers that His Father now gives “the true bread from heaven.” Many read the manna Israel ate in the wilderness as a type, and Christ as the bread it pointed to, as He goes on to say: “I am the bread of life.”

figure.name: Type
figure.means: Christ, the bread the Father gives, to which the manna of the wilderness pointed ahead

notes.evidence: Henry: Christ tells them of the true manna, of which the manna was a type, but a shadow and figure. Clarke: the manna was not the true bread but merely a type of it, and Christ was typified by it. Benson: the manna was only a symbolical representation of the true, heavenly bread the Father now gives.

cites.quote: He informs them concerning the true manna, of which that was a type: But my Father giveth you the true bread from heaven; that which is truly and properly the bread from heaven, of which the manna was but a shadow and figure
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: That this bread was not the true bread, but was merely a type of it. … That himself is that heavenly nourishment of which he spake, and who was typified by the manna in the desert.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: neither was the manna bread from heaven, though it be so called by the psalmist, on account of the thing which it typified … he now giveth you the true spiritual, heavenly bread, of which the manna was only a symbolical representation
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: Jesus leaves His question about ascending unfinished
notes.about: When many disciples take offense at His words, Jesus speaks of the day they may “see the Son of Man ascend to where He was before,” and does not finish the thought. What would follow is left unsaid; it can be read as asking whether they would believe even then.

figure.name: Aposiopesis
figure.words: if you see the Son of Man ascend to where He was before
figure.means: the end is left unsaid: would they believe then, or take still greater offense

original.note: In John's Greek the question is only an “if” clause (ean), with no main clause after it; English supplies “what will happen.”

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists John 6:62 under Ellipsis and again under Aposiopesis, since more is implied than any words could supply. Bengel says the if-clause leaves its conclusion to be understood, with far greater things to follow. Henry asks what then, and offers ways the sentence may be completed.
notes.limit: The writers fill in the unsaid end differently: that the hearers would be offended still more, or would then be satisfied; one says more is meant than any words could supply.

cites.quote: “And if ye shall see the Son of Man ascend up where he was before--?” This has already been referred to under Ellipsis (see p. 54). But something more is implied; more than can be supplied by any specific words, such as, “Will ye believe then?” For He did afterwards ascend up, but they still refused to believe!
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: ἐάν, if, has as the Apodosis to be understood, what shall be? ... That is, there are far greater things, which will follow: if ye do not believe this, how would you believe those things, if I were to tell you them?
cites.read: Bible Hub's transcription, at https://biblehub.com/commentaries/bengel/john/6.htm

cites.quote: And what then? First, "If I should tell you of that, surely it would much more offend you, and you would think my pretensions too high indeed. ... Or, Thirdly, "When you see that, or hear it from those that shall see it, surely then you will be satisfied.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: The sheepfold, the gate and the good shepherd
notes.about: Jesus pictures a sheepfold. Thieves climb in another way, but the shepherd enters by the gate, and his sheep know his voice. When His hearers do not understand, He opens the picture: He is the gate for the sheep, and the good shepherd who lays down His life for them.

figure.name: Allegory
figure.words: whoever does not enter the sheepfold by the gate
figure.means: God's people as a fold, entered only through Christ the gate and led by Him as their shepherd, while false leaders climb in another way

original.note: In John's Greek the word for this illustration in verse 6 is paroimia, a wide word for figurative speech; it is not the word usually rendered parable.

notes.evidence: H. W. Watkins (Ellicott's Commentary) renders the word in verse 6 as allegory, not parable, and warns that not every detail, such as the gatekeeper, is to be pressed. Barnes reads the fold as God's people and the door as Christ, and says the Pharisees came in another way. Henry calls it a figurative discourse in which the fold is the church, and Christ makes Himself both the door and the shepherd.
notes.limit: Two of these writers call it a parable or a similitude, and one warns against pressing every detail, such as the gatekeeper.

cites.quote: Better, this allegory spake Jesus unto them. The word rendered “parable” is the wider word (παροιμία, paroimia ) which includes every kind of figurative and proverbial teaching ... the interpretation of every point in the history of the material facts ( e.g., “ the porter” in Joh 10:3 ) is not always to be pressed.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: The true vine: a picture carried through
notes.about: Jesus carries one picture through these verses. He is the true vine and His Father the keeper of the vineyard; the disciples are the branches. Branches that bear fruit are pruned to bear more, and a branch that does not remain in Him withers and is burned.

figure.name: Allegory
figure.means: Christ, the source of all His people's life and fruit; the Father tends and prunes them, and removes fruitless branches

notes.evidence: H. W. Watkins (Ellicott's Commentary) calls the passage an allegory, in which the branches in view are true and false Christians. Calvin finds three main parts in the comparison and warns against pressing every property of the vine. Barnes: as a vine feeds its branches, Jesus is the source of His disciples' strength. Henry: Christ is the vine, believers the branches, the Father the husbandman.
notes.limit: One of these writers calls it a similitude, and another reads it for its main points only, not for each feature of a vine.

cites.quote: It has been implied, but not directly stated, that they are the branches. ... The persons thought of all through this allegory are true and false Christians

notes.short: “They will keep yours”: more is meant than said
notes.about: Jesus says “if they kept My word, they will keep yours as well,” but He means more than the words say. The world had refused His word, and it would refuse theirs just as surely: His disciples could look for no better hearing than He had.

figure.name: Meiosis
figure.words: if they kept My word, they will keep yours as well
figure.means: the world that refused His word will refuse the disciples' word just as surely

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Meiosis (a belittling): as surely as they have not kept His saying, they will not keep the disciples', and he says the whole context shows this must be the figure. Henry says Christ means they will regard the disciples' sayings no more than they have regarded and kept His.

cites.quote: “If they have kept my saying, they will keep yours also,” i.e., as surely as they have NOT kept my saying, they will not keep yours. The whole context shows that this must be the figure of Meiosis.
